newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU meets to discuss tricky pensions issue.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU meets to discuss tricky pensions issue.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) met on Wednesday to work out a common line on pensions reform, an issue that has split the party and put his longest-serving minister in the firing line.
Going into a CDU executive meeting, however, Kohl said the expected no final decision to adopt Labour Minister Norbert Bluem's plans to rejig Germany's old-age pension scheme.
"This is a first discussion of the subject, and Bluem's proposals are a good working basis," Kohl said. "But that doesn't mean that all points will be accepted by the party."
Bluem's pensions plans would leave the pay-as-you-go German system little changed, cutting pensions and raising contributions to cope with the "greying" of the country's 80 million population.
But, by failing to adopt radical financing alternatives, Bluem has angered young CDU radicals.

By calling for a rise in value-added tax to finance a "family fund" of non-related welfare items, the Bluem plan clashed directly with coalition tax reforms drawn up under Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

Isolated on taxes, Bluem -- in Kohl's cabinet since 1982 -- appeared last week to be close to resigning. But his proposals won majority backing from CDU pensions experts on Monday, with some minor changes.

The key points of the plan remain intact: Pensions would fall to 64 percent of average net wages by 2030 from 70 percent now. Contributions would rise to 22.9 percent from 20.3 percent -- already a record.
Both the CDU and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) are flirting with cross-party talks on pensions and tax reforms.
But the SPD is waiting for the Kohl party to finalise its pensions position before committing to negotiations.
The threat of isolation has quieted the two smaller parties in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition, which had been sharply critical of Bluem's proposals.

Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) -- who on Tuesday pledged renewed loyalty to Kohl -- on Wednesday toned down demands for new taxes on pensions contained in Waigel's tax reform package.
"My whole world view does not depend on it," FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told the Die Zeit weekly.

But Gerhardt called for urgent measures to build capital reserves in the compulsory state pensions scheme -- which now operates on a hand-to-mouth basis -- and said other investments like shares should have equal tax treatment.
Kohl said the Bluem plan would be discussed with coalition partners the FDP and Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) over the coming weeks.
